clue.text: Teacher of no practical use

definitions.meaning: a job title for someone who teaches at a university
describes a question or argument that is purely theoretical, with no bearing on anything real

explanation.walkthrough: One word wearing two parts of speech, run together with nothing between them. The joke is that the second reading is a quiet insult aimed at the first.
explanation.definitionFit: An academic is a university teacher; as an adjective the word means purely theoretical, an argument with no bearing on anything real.

clue.text: Opening above large part of church

indicators.note: In a down entry whatever stands higher is written first, so this word fixes which piece leads.

parts.note: an opening is a chance, an opportunity
L = large, the clothing-size abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' looks architectural in a clue about churches and turns out to mean a stroke of luck. L for large comes off a shirt collar and is worth filing away.
explanation.definitionFit: The chancel is the space round the altar at the east end of a church, kept for clergy and choir.

clue.text: Unpleasant fluid dilutes fast

indicators.note: A fluid holds no shape of its own, so what it describes will not stay in the order it was given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like the small print on a bottle, which is exactly why 'fluid' slips past as a description of the liquid rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Distasteful means offensive to taste or feeling, a close everyday synonym for 'unpleasant' carrying a stronger note of moral disapproval.

clue.text: Bulk energy shot

parts.note: bulk and mass are both sheer quantity of matter
E = energy, the physicist's abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulk energy' reads as one phrase about power supply and is two separate pieces. The billiards word is properly spelt with an accent, which the grid simply drops.
explanation.definitionFit: A masse is a billiards stroke played with the cue held almost upright to curve the ball, so 'shot' names it by its class.

clue.text: Fancy that guy being put into care, possibly

indicators.note: Putting one thing into another is placing it bodily inside, so the shorter piece ends up buried in the longer.
'Possibly' says the word before it is only one arrangement of its letters, and some other arrangement is wanted.

parts.note: the letters of CARE rearranged
that guy is him

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy that guy' reads as a swoon and is really the definition bumping straight into the wordplay. Short ordinary words like 'care' are the ones setters most like to jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is an idle fancy or wild imagining, the noun sense of 'fancy' that survives mainly in books and crosswords.

clue.text: Obscure, extremely bumptious words on book jackets

parts.note: to obscure something is to blur it

indicators.note: The extremes of a word are its two far ends, so only the outermost letter at each end is taken.

parts.note: the outer letters of B-umptiou-S

explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' is a verb here, not an adjective, and that switch is most of the difficulty. The surface pretends the whole clue is about a pompous author.
explanation.definitionFit: Blurbs are the puffing descriptions printed on a dust jacket to sell a book, so the definition names them by where they appear.

clue.text: Person providing protection for state is working very hard

indicators.note: To shelter something is to close round it, so one word wraps itself entirely about another.

parts.note: a being is a person, a living creature
to aver is to state something as fact

explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'person' as a being rather than a named someone is the step that unlocks this. Beavering away is the idiom the definition leans on, from the animal's proverbial industry.
explanation.definitionFit: To beaver away is to toil without pause, so the participle stands in exactly for 'working very hard' in its idiomatic sense.

clue.text: Learning institution's subdivision reduced in size by 25%

indicators.note: A quarter off a four-letter word is one letter gone, and what goes is the letter at the end.

parts.note: a unit is a subdivision of something larger

explanation.walkthrough: The percentage is the joke - read '25%' as arithmetic performed on the word, not as a description of a department being cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Uni is the British colloquial shortening of university, and a university is the learning institution the phrase points at.

clue.text: Gathered together and had late-morning meal right away

indicators.note: 'Away' is the direction a thing goes when it is taken off, so the letter named just before it leaves.

parts.note: brunch is the meal between breakfast and lunch
R = right, the standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: Brunch is a portmanteau of breakfast and lunch, which is why 'late-morning meal' points at it so precisely. R for right pairs with L for left all over crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Things bunched are drawn into a clump, so 'gathered together' is the plain past-tense synonym - what a florist does to flowers.

clue.text: Two idiots initiating one state shooting, perhaps

parts.note: an ass is an idiot, and the clue asks for two of them

indicators.note: To initiate is to begin, so what is wanted is the opening letter of the word that follows.

parts.note: the initial letter of 'one'
a nation is a state

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a news bulletin and every word of it is doing something else: 'state' is an ordinary country and the idiots are donkeys.
explanation.definitionFit: The murder of a public figure is an assassination, and gunfire is one common method, so the definition works by example rather than by kind.

clue.text: Dispose of the last bit of homemade pickle

parts.note: to scrap a thing is to dispose of it

indicators.note: The final bit of a word is its closing letter and nothing more.

parts.note: the last letter of 'homemade'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pickle' is the definition and has nothing to do with food: a scrape is a spot of bother. The surface leans hard on the homemade-chutney reading to hide that.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrape is an awkward fix you have got yourself into, the same informal sense in which someone is in a pickle.

clue.text: Perception absolutely possessed by rowing crew

indicators.note: To be possessed by something is to be held within it, so one word sits inside the other.

parts.note: an eight is a racing crew of eight rowers
'absolutely' is an emphatic yes

explanation.walkthrough: An eight for a rowing crew is one of the most reliable pieces of crossword vocabulary, and 'absolutely' as a word of agreement is the other half worth remembering.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyesight is the faculty of seeing, so 'perception' names it by the wider class of taking the world in through a sense.

clue.text: Popular pink avatar

parts.note: what is popular is in, as in fashion
a carnation is a variety of pink, the garden flower

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, no indicator, and the whole difficulty is that 'pink' is a flower rather than a colour. 'Avatar' is wanted in its older Hindu sense, not the film.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu belief an avatar is a deity's bodily descent into the world, which is precisely an incarnation - spirit given flesh.

clue.text: International clothing label about to bring on board rubbish celebrities

indicators.note: 'About' means turned round, so the letters just assembled are read back the other way.
Bringing something on board is taking it inside, so a word is loaded into the middle of what is already there.

parts.note: I = international, the standard abbreviation
the label sewn into a garment is its tag
litter is rubbish dropped about the place

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothing label' invites you to name a fashion house and means the thing sewn inside a collar. 'On board' is the setter's usual way of saying something is taken inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The glitterati are the fashionable famous, so the definition is a plain synonym with the glamour and the faint sneer already built in.

clue.text: She acts single, following couple of males in certain direction

definitions.note: 'She acts' is a sentence rather than a noun phrase, so it describes the answer - a film actress - instead of standing in for her.

indicators.note: What follows comes afterwards, so this piece is written after everything already assembled.
This little word puts a piece bodily within another rather than beside it.

parts.note: east is one of the four points of the compass
M = male, and a couple of them is MM
a single of anything is one

explanation.walkthrough: The clue never says 'actress' - two words do the same job while reading as gossip about someone's love life. 'Certain direction' stays vague until the letters force the compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is an American film actress, Oscar-winning star of La La Land and Poor Things, named here by her profession.

clue.text: System of rules requiring constant, dedicated work?

parts.note: C = constant, the standard symbol in mathematics
an ode is a poem written in someone's honour

explanation.walkthrough: An ode is dedicated to its subject, which is what makes 'dedicated work' fair rather than merely flattering. The question mark flags that stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A code is a body of rules - the highway code, a legal code - so the civil sense is wanted, not the secret-writing one.

clue.text: Trashy, somewhat lumpen affair

indicators.note: 'Somewhat' means only part of what follows is wanted, and that part runs unbroken through the words.

parts.note: the answer sits unbroken across the join between these two words

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden answers love a join between two words like this, because the eye reads whole words and steps straight over the seam where the letters actually are.
explanation.definitionFit: Naff is British slang for tacky and in poor taste, which is what 'trashy' says of clothes, gifts or television.

clue.text: Determined 80s pop star

definitions.note: The second definition only works once the letters are respaced into two words, so it defines the string rather than the word.
definitions.meaning: describes someone who will not be moved from a position, whatever the pressure
an early-80s New Romantic frontman, best known for 'Stand and Deliver' — his stage name reads as two words

explanation.walkthrough: Respacing an ordinary word into a name is one of the oldest tricks in the book, and a two-word pop star is the perfect place to hide it.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant means immovably determined, from an old name for the hardest of stones; split differently the same letters name the New Romantic singer.

clue.text: Wild animal rage coming from the top dogs?

indicators.note: Untamed things are out of order by nature, so the letters beside this word refuse to stay where they were put.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild animal rage' is a complete picture in three words, which is what makes it so hard to see the last two as raw material rather than scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: Managerial describes whatever issues from managers, and 'top dogs' is slang for the people in charge, so the adjective fits their orders exactly.

clue.text: Frost ultimately breaks hole in crumbling relic

indicators.note: Something crumbling is falling apart into loose pieces, which is what happens here to the order of the letters.
To break into somewhere is to force your way inside, so this letter lands in among the rest.

parts.note: the six letters of HOLE IN, rearranged

indicators.note: Ultimately means at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word before is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of 'Frost'

explanation.walkthrough: Frost is capitalised so it reads as a surname, and it is only weather. The picture the surface paints - ice splitting a ruin - is the picture archaeology would give you too.
explanation.definitionFit: A neolith is a New Stone Age implement, so 'relic' names it by the class of surviving ancient object it belongs to.

clue.text: Supplies of first-class horses

parts.note: A1 is top grade, so first-class gives A
a mount is a horse you ride

explanation.walkthrough: A mount is the rider's word for a horse rather than the animal itself, and A for first-class comes from A1, the shipping register's top rating.
explanation.definitionFit: Amounts are quantities on hand, so the definition matches in its plural noun sense - stocks of a thing available, not the verb.

clue.text: Satellite phone? It's crazily old

parts.note: to phone someone is to call them

indicators.note: Doing anything crazily is doing it with no regard for order, so these letters land anyhow.

parts.note: three letters, the apostrophe dropping out
O = old, the standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Satellite phone' is lovely misdirection: two words that belong together in life and to opposite halves of the clue. The answer is one of Jupiter's moons.
explanation.definitionFit: Callisto is one of Jupiter's four Galilean moons, so the definition works by class in the astronomical sense rather than the man-made one.

clue.text: Drawer primarily containing fabric

indicators.note: Primarily points at what comes first, so only the opening letter of the next word is used.

parts.note: the first letter of 'containing'
rayon is a manufactured fabric

explanation.walkthrough: 'Containing' looks every inch like an instruction to put one thing inside another, and it is really a word being asked for its opening letter. That double bluff is the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A crayon is a stick of coloured wax used for drawing, so the definition names it as the thing that draws rather than a person who does.

clue.text: Head of cabbage with tough green leaves

definitions.note: Chard is a mass noun - you eat chard, not chards - so the plural 'leaves' describes the vegetable rather than counting it.

indicators.note: The head of a word is its front, so just the opening letter is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of 'cabbage'
a tough customer is a hard one

explanation.walkthrough: A head of cabbage is a real thing you can buy, which is what lets the instruction pass as scenery. The surface never leaves the vegetable patch.
explanation.definitionFit: Chard is a beet grown for its broad glossy foliage rather than its root, so it reaches the table as exactly that.

clue.text: Domineering writer from Rome, maybe changing sides?

indicators.note: Swapping one side for the other means left becomes right, and each of those has its own one-letter abbreviation.

parts.note: an author is a writer
someone from Rome might be an ITALIAN, whose L (left) becomes R (right)

explanation.walkthrough: L for left and R for right is a swap worth memorising, and 'changing sides' is one of several ways a setter can ask for it. Rome supplies the nationality by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Authoritarian describes a ruler or a manner that demands obedience, so 'domineering' is a close adjectival synonym with a political edge.

clue.text: Drink in the bar periodically

indicators.note: Something done periodically recurs at regular intervals, so letters are picked at a steady step through the words.

parts.note: every second letter of T-h-E-b-A-r

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' and 'drink' hold the surface together while the letters come from somewhere else entirely. Taking every other letter is one of the commonest extractions there is.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the everyday British cuppa, so the definition works by class - the beverage, not the evening meal the word also names.

clue.text: A kid taking it easy

parts.note: the clue's own A, used as itself
to kid someone is to tease them

explanation.walkthrough: A bare 'A' at the start of a clue is nearly always itself, which is why it disappears so easily. 'Kid' is a verb here, not a child.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer means relaxed and unhurried, matching the definition as a whole phrase; it is also the parade-ground order to stand down.

clue.text: Fun-loving sort of mafia boss involved in robbery

indicators.note: To be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so one word goes within the other.

parts.note: a heist is a planned robbery
don is the title of a mafia chief, borrowed from Sicilian usage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' means a person here rather than a kind of thing, which is what keeps the definition from looking like one. The surface stays entirely inside the crime film.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist treats pleasure as the point of life, so the definition names the person by the appetite that defines them.
